exercises.prompt: Diego is designing a bird feeder. His cardboard prototype holds plenty of seed, but in his test the seed got soaked when he sprinkled water on it to imitate rain. What should he do **next**?

options.label: Improve the design, for example by adding a roof, and test again.
options.feedback: Yes. The test has taught him something; the next step is to change the design and go round the loop again.

options.label: Start making the final feeder from wood straight away.
options.feedback: Not yet. The design has just failed a test. Making it in wood would only produce a sturdier feeder with soggy seed.

options.label: Give up: the design has failed.
options.feedback: Not yet. A failed test is information, not a failure. That is what prototypes are for.

options.label: Delete the rain test from his list of requirements.
options.feedback: Not yet. Birds feed outdoors, where it rains. Removing a real requirement because it is hard to meet just hides the problem.

hints: The design cycle goes: problem, ideas, prototype, test, improve, and round again.
Which step comes straight after a test that showed a problem?
exercises.solution: After **test** comes **improve**. Diego has learned that the seed needs protecting from rain, so he changes the design (a roof, or a tray with drainage holes), makes a new prototype and tests it again. Only when the design passes every test should he make the final version. Notice how cheap the lesson was: he learned it with cardboard and a few drops of water.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are **good** workshop habits? Choose all that apply.

options.label: Wearing safety glasses while a friend is drilling nearby, even though you are only watching.
options.feedback: Yes. Chips fly well beyond the drill, so everyone nearby protects their eyes.

options.label: Tying back long hair before using a drill.
options.feedback: Yes. Hair, loose sleeves and dangling jewellery can be caught by a spinning drill and pull you in.

options.label: Taking the guard off a machine so you can see the work better.
options.feedback: Not this one. Guards exist to keep hands away from cutting and moving parts. If you cannot see the work, ask a supervisor; never remove a guard.

options.label: Clamping a piece of wood before sawing it, and cutting away from your body.
options.feedback: Yes. A clamp holds the work so both your hands stay well away from the blade.

options.label: Wearing loose gloves while using a pillar drill.
options.feedback: Not this one. A glove can be caught by the spinning bit and drag your hand in. Gloves are for handling sharp sheets or rough timber, not for working at a rotating machine.

hints: For each habit, ask: does it keep fingers, eyes and hair away from danger, or bring them closer?
Three of the five are good habits. Think carefully about anything loose near a spinning part.
exercises.solution: Good habits: **(a)** eye protection for everyone nearby, **(b)** tying back long hair, and **(d)** clamping the work and cutting away from yourself. Bad habits: **(c)** removing a guard, which takes away the protection that works even when you are not paying attention, and **(e)** loose gloves at a rotating machine, which can be caught and pull your hand in. Gloves are useful in a workshop, but for carrying sharp sheet metal or rough wood, not near spinning tools.

exercises.prompt: A pasta maker pushes dough through a plate with shaped holes, and long pasta tubes come out the other side. Which family of making is this most like?

options.label: Shaping: the dough changes form without any being removed. (This process is called extrusion.)
options.feedback: Yes. Extrusion squeezes material through a shaped hole, exactly like aluminium window frames and plastic pipes are made.

options.label: Cutting: material is taken away.
options.feedback: Not yet. No dough is cut away and thrown out; all of it comes through the plate in a new shape.

options.label: Casting: liquid is poured into a mould and left to harden.
options.feedback: Not yet. The dough is a soft solid being pushed through a hole, not a liquid filling a closed mould.

options.label: 3D printing: the part is built up layer by layer.
options.feedback: Not yet. The pasta comes out as one continuous piece, not as stacked layers.

hints: Is any material removed? Is it poured as a liquid? Is it built in layers?
The lesson compared one shaping process to toothpaste coming out of a tube.
exercises.solution: No dough is removed (so it is not cutting), it is not a liquid hardening in a closed mould (not casting), and it is not built layer by layer (not 3D printing). The dough is forced through a shaped hole and comes out with that shape: this is **extrusion**, one of the **shaping** processes. Factories extrude aluminium window frames, plastic pipes and many other long parts with the same cross-section all along their length.

exercises.prompt: A greenhouse frame needs long, straight bars with the same detailed cross-section all along them. They must be light, must not rust when they are outdoors all year, and hundreds of metres are needed. Which choice fits best?

options.label: Extruded aluminium.
options.feedback: Yes. Aluminium is light and resists corrosion, and extrusion makes long bars with a complicated cross-section quickly and cheaply.

options.label: 3D-printed plastic.
options.feedback: Not yet. Printing hundreds of metres of bar would take a very long time, and many printing plastics weaken in sunlight.

options.label: Cast iron.
options.feedback: Not yet. Cast iron is heavy, rusts unless protected, and is brittle: a poor choice for long, slender bars.

options.label: Carbon-fibre composite, made by hand.
options.feedback: Not yet. It is light and stiff, but far too expensive and slow to make for hundreds of metres of simple frame.

hints: Check each option against all three requirements: light, does not rust, and quick to make in long lengths.
Which process makes long parts with the same cross-section all along them?
exercises.solution: Go through the requirements one by one. **Light** rules out cast iron. **Does not rust outdoors** rules out cast iron again, and favours aluminium. **Hundreds of metres, quickly and cheaply** rules out 3D printing and hand-made carbon fibre. **Same cross-section all along** is exactly what extrusion makes. So the answer is **extruded aluminium**, which is indeed what most greenhouse and window frames are made of.

exercises.prompt: A 3D printer builds a model figure 45 mm tall, in layers 0.15 mm thick. How many layers does it print?

feedback.message: Not yet: check the decimal point. 0.15 mm is less than a fifth of a millimetre, so there are many more layers than millimetres.
Not yet: that is ten times too many. Check your division: 45 ÷ 0.15.

hints: Number of layers = height ÷ thickness of one layer.
exercises.solution: Number of layers = 45 ÷ 0.15 = 4500 ÷ 15 = **300** layers. If each layer takes about 40 seconds, the print takes 300 × 40 = 12 000 seconds, which is 200 minutes, or 3 hours and 20 minutes. Thinner layers give a smoother surface but take longer, so choosing the layer thickness is itself a small design decision.

exercises.prompt:
A company can 3D print a plastic clip for 2.00 euros each, or pay 9000 euros for an injection mould and then make each clip for 0.50 euros.

At how many clips do the two ways cost **exactly the same**?

feedback.message: Not yet: 9000 ÷ 2.00 ignores the 0.50 euros each moulded clip still costs. Use the difference between the two prices per clip.
Not yet: 9000 ÷ 0.50 uses only the moulded price. Each moulded clip saves 2.00 − 0.50 euros compared with printing.

hints: Each moulded clip is cheaper than a printed one by 2.00 − 0.50 = 1.50 euros.
How many clips, each saving 1.50 euros, does it take to pay back the 9000-euro mould?
exercises.solution:
Each moulded clip saves 2.00 − 0.50 = 1.50 euros compared with printing. The mould costs 9000 euros, so it has paid for itself after 9000 ÷ 1.50 = **6000** clips.

Check: printing 6000 clips costs 6000 × 2.00 = 12 000 euros; moulding costs 9000 + 6000 × 0.50 = 12 000 euros. The same. For fewer clips, printing is cheaper; for more, moulding is.

exercises.prompt: A drawing says a hole must be **25 ± 0.2** mm across. A factory measures five holes. Which one is **acceptable**?

options.label: 24.85 mm
options.feedback: Yes. 24.85 is between 24.8 and 25.2, so it is inside the tolerance.

options.label: 24.70 mm
options.feedback: Not yet. The smallest acceptable size is 25 − 0.2 = 24.8 mm, and 24.70 is smaller than that.

options.label: 25.30 mm
options.feedback: Not yet. The largest acceptable size is 25 + 0.2 = 25.2 mm, and 25.30 is bigger than that.

options.label: 25.25 mm
options.feedback: Not yet, though close. The limit is 25.2 mm, and 25.25 is just over it.

hints: Work out the smallest and largest acceptable sizes, then check each measurement.
exercises.solution: The tolerance allows sizes from 25 − 0.2 = **24.8 mm** up to 25 + 0.2 = **25.2 mm**. Only **24.85 mm** lies in that range. 24.70 is too small; 25.30 and 25.25 are too big. A pin or bolt designed to fit this hole would be drawn with its own tolerance, chosen so that every acceptable pin fits every acceptable hole.

exercises.tests:
assert printing_cost(1) is not ..., "Replace the ... in printing_cost with a calculation."
assert moulding_cost(1) is not ..., "Replace the ... in moulding_cost with a calculation."
assert abs(printing_cost(10) - 30) < 1e-9, "Not yet: printing 10 stands at 3.00 each should cost 30."
assert abs(moulding_cost(10) - 6004) < 1e-9, "Not yet: moulding 10 stands should cost 6000 + 10 x 0.40 = 6004."
assert abs(moulding_cost(0) - 6000) < 1e-9, "Not yet: even with no stands, the mould still costs 6000."
assert cheaper(10) == "printing", "Not yet: for 10 stands, printing is far cheaper."
assert cheaper(2000) == "printing", "Not yet: for 2000 stands, printing (6000) is still cheaper than moulding (6800)."
assert cheaper(3000) == "moulding", "Not yet: for 3000 stands, moulding (7200) is cheaper than printing (9000)."
assert cheaper(100000) == "moulding"
hints: Printing has no start-up cost: the total is just the number of stands times the price of one.
Moulding has a start-up cost: `6000 + n * 0.40`.
In `cheaper`, compare the two totals: `if printing_cost(n) < moulding_cost(n):`.
